lessons.title: When the police stop you
lessons.summary: What turns a stop into an arrest, the three things you can ask for, and the clock that starts the moment you are no longer free to go.

sections.keypoint: Most people will never read a contract in a courtroom; many will meet a police officer.

body.text: Most people will never read a contract in a court room. Many will meet a police officer. This lesson is about that meeting, in the order it happens.
It is written for the person it happens to, and for the family at home waiting for news. You need no legal training to follow it.

sections.keypoint: Being stopped and questioned is not an arrest — an arrest is when you are no longer free to leave.

body.text: Faizal drives a lorry in Ipoh. One night the police stop him at a roadblock. They ask for his identity card and look in the cab.
Nothing has happened to Faizal in law yet. He has been stopped and questioned. When the officers finish, he drives away.
Being stopped and questioned is not an arrest. An arrest is the point at which a person is taken into custody and is no longer free to leave.
The line is drawn by control, not by words. Nobody has to say the word arrest. If you are cuffed, held, or put in a vehicle, you are under arrest whatever it is called.

body.title: The one question that tells you which it is
body.caption: Nobody has to say the word arrest. The line is drawn by control. If you are cuffed, held, or put in a vehicle, you are under arrest whatever anyone calls it.
body.alt: A question — are you free to walk away? — branching two ways. Yes: you have been stopped and questioned, and in law nothing has happened to you yet. No, because you are cuffed, held or put in a vehicle: you are under arrest, and the protections that follow an arrest apply.
body.question: Are you free to walk away?

branches.label: Stopped and questioned
branches.note: in law, nothing has happened yet

sections.keypoint: For a seizable offence police may arrest without a warrant; otherwise one is generally needed.

body.text: An arrest takes away your liberty. The officer takes you into custody, either by touching you or because you submit and go along.
For a seizable offence a police officer may arrest without a warrant. For other offences a warrant or an order is generally needed.
A seizable offence is simply one the Code marks for arrest without a warrant. Which offences those are is looked up in the First Schedule, not worked out by argument.

Two neighbours fight outside a kedai runcit. One is arrested at the scene. The other is told to come to the station on Friday. The difference is how the Code classifies each offence, not who shouted louder.

sections.keypoint: Ask for three things: the grounds, a lawyer, and to tell your family.

body.text: The Constitution gives an arrested person rights that start at once. They are short, and they are worth knowing by heart.
Article 5(3): a person arrested shall be informed as soon as may be of the grounds of his arrest. He shall also be allowed to consult and be defended by a lawyer of his choice.
The Criminal Procedure Code adds a right people forget. Somebody at home may be told where you are.
The Code requires the police to let an arrested person contact a relative or friend, and a lawyer of his choice.

items: Ask what offence you are being held for. You are entitled to be told.
Ask for someone at home to be told where you are.
Ask for a lawyer, by name if you have one.
Ask for the officer's name and the station you are being taken to.

body.text: When the right to a lawyer must be honoured is fought over in the courts. Police often say later. Ask anyway, ask again, and have someone write down each time you asked.

sections.keypoint: Twenty-four hours, then a Magistrate. That clock is in the Constitution, not just the Code.

body.text: The most useful number in this module is twenty-four. It is the limit on police detention without a Magistrate.
Article 5(4): a person arrested and not released shall be produced before a Magistrate within twenty-four hours, and shall not be detained further without the Magistrate's authority.
Faizal is arrested at nine on Sunday night. By nine on Monday night he must be released or taken before a Magistrate. If neither has happened, his family should be asking why.
The twenty-four hours leaves out the time needed to travel to the Magistrate. In a rural district that can matter. It is not a licence for a second night in the lock-up.

sections.keypoint: You must answer truthfully, but not a question whose answer would expose you to a charge.

body.text: People assume they must answer everything, or that they may answer nothing. Neither is the Malaysian position.
A person questioned by the police must answer truthfully. He need not answer a question whose answer would expose him to a criminal charge or a penalty.
body.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593), provisions on police statements

body.text: So your name and address are not optional. Explaining where the phone in your bag came from is a different matter.
A statement given to the police can be used later. Never sign one you have not read. If you cannot read it, say so and ask for it to be read out to you.

sections.keypoint: Write down the times afterwards — memory of a bad night is what the later argument turns on.

body.text: Whatever happens, someone should keep a note. Memory of a bad night is unreliable, and the times are what the arguments later turn on.

items: The time and place of the stop, and the time of the arrest.
What you were told, and what you asked for.
The names or numbers of the officers, and the station.
Every time a lawyer or a phone call was requested, and the answer given.

body.text: If the family cannot afford a lawyer, ask about the legal aid centre run by the Bar in the State. There is also a government legal aid scheme.

sections.keypoint: Nobody memorises their rights at eleven at night, which is why these five cards go in first.

body.text: Five cards. They are the ones to have by heart before you need them, because nobody memorises rights at eleven at night in a police station.
Then work the guided problem, which walks you through one arrest step by step. After that, the lesson From arrest to charge takes the classifications properly.

lessons.source: Federal Constitution Arts 5(3) and 5(4); Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593), including the First Schedule and s 28A.
lessons.verify: Read Arts 5(3) and 5(4) in a current reprint of the Federal Constitution. The rights on arrest in the Criminal Procedure Code have been amended more than once, so read s 28A in a current reprint before relying on the detail here. The case law on when access to a lawyer must be allowed is live and contested — read it in full rather than in summary.

quiz.q: When does a police stop become an arrest?
options: When you are taken into custody and are no longer free to leave
When the officer says the word arrest
When handcuffs are used
When you reach the police station
quiz.why: It turns on control, not on any form of words. Handcuffs are not needed either.
quiz.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593); arrest turns on custody and control

quiz.q: What must you be told when you are arrested?
options: The grounds of your arrest, as soon as may be
The name of the investigating officer
The maximum sentence you face
Nothing at all until you are charged
quiz.why: Article 5(3) says so. The trap is thinking the right only starts at the charge.
quiz.source: Federal Constitution Art 5(3)

quiz.q: After an arrest, who may you ask to contact?
options: A lawyer only
A relative only
Nobody until questioning has finished
A lawyer of your choice, and a relative or friend
quiz.why: Article 5(3) gives you the lawyer; the Code adds the relative or friend. Police often say later, so ask again and note the time.
quiz.source: Federal Constitution Art 5(3); Criminal Procedure Code s 28A

quiz.q: How long may the police hold you before a Magistrate must see you?
options: Forty-eight hours
Seven days
Twenty-four hours
Until the investigation is finished
quiz.why: Article 5(4). Longer needs a Magistrate's order, and travel time to the Magistrate is not counted.
quiz.source: Federal Constitution Art 5(4)

quiz.q: Must you answer a police question if the answer would expose you to a charge?
options: No, though you must answer other questions truthfully
Yes, always
No, and you need not answer anything at all
Only if a lawyer is present
quiz.why: The Code asks for truthful answers but protects you from ones that would incriminate you. Refusing to say anything at all is not the rule.
quiz.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593); the protection against self-incriminating answers

quiz.q: Arrested at nine on Sunday night, still in the lock-up at noon on Tuesday, no Magistrate seen. What is the position?
options: It is lawful because the investigation is not finished
It is lawful if a senior officer approved it
It is lawful for the first three days
The detention has run past the constitutional limit
quiz.why: Twenty-four hours is the limit without a Magistrate, and only a remand order extends it.
quiz.source: Federal Constitution Art 5(4)

lessons.title: The lock-up, the charge and the first day in court
lessons.summary: Remand, the charge read out, the plea, and what bail and a surety really are — written for the family in the public gallery.

sections.keypoint: A night in the lock-up ends one of three ways, and knowing which tells you what to do next.
sections.h: Three roads out of the lock-up

body.text: A night in the lock-up ends in one of three ways. Knowing which one you are in tells you what to do next.

items: Released with no charge. Sometimes with a warning, sometimes with nothing said at all.
Released on police bail, with a date to come back to the station.
Taken before a Magistrate, who is asked to allow the police more time.

body.text: The third road is the remand hearing. It is where families most often turn up with no idea what is about to happen.

body.title: Which road you are on
body.caption: Knowing which of the three you are in tells you what to do next. Families most often arrive with no idea that the third one is about to happen.
body.alt: A question — how does the night end? — branching three ways. Released with no charge, sometimes with a warning. Released on police bail, with a date to come back to the station. Or taken before a Magistrate, who is asked to allow the police more time.
body.question: How does the night end?

branches.label: Released
branches.note: a warning, or nothing said at all

sections.keypoint: Beyond twenty-four hours needs a Magistrate's remand order, made for the investigation.

body.text: Remand means holding a person while the police investigate. After the first twenty-four hours only a Magistrate can allow it.
Detention beyond twenty-four hours needs a remand order from a Magistrate. It is made for the investigation, and for the period the Magistrate thinks fit.
The hearing is short and is often held in a small room. The investigating officer says why more time is needed. The person arrested may speak, and so may a lawyer.
Danial is nineteen and has never been arrested. The police ask for seven days. His lawyer points out that the phone has already been seized, so four days would do. The Magistrate gives four.
Nobody is deciding guilt at a remand hearing. Arguing that Danial did not do it is the wrong argument. The question is whether more detention is really needed.

sections.keypoint: A charge must give enough detail of time, place and person to be answered.

body.text: A charge is the written accusation read out in court. It is the first document in the case that truly belongs to the accused.
A charge must state the offence, with enough detail of time, place and person for the accused to know what he is answering.
body.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593), provisions on the form of charges

body.text: Theft of a mobile phone belonging to Puan Lim, at a shop on Jalan Melaka, on 3 March. That is enough. Theft of something, somewhere in Melaka, some time last year is not.
The charge is read in a language the accused understands. If it is not understood, say so before pleading, not afterwards.

sections.keypoint: Two real answers to a charge, and pleading guilty to get it over with is a decision with consequences.

body.text: Once the charge is read the court asks for a plea. There are two real answers.

items: Guilty. The court may convict at once, and the next step is sentence.
Not guilty, usually said in court as claiming trial. The prosecution must then prove the charge.

body.text: A guilty plea is not simply accepted. The court checks that the accused understands the charge and admits the facts behind it.
People plead guilty to get out of the lock-up sooner. It is the most expensive short cut in this module. A conviction stays on the record, and the sentence can be heavier than the wait.

sections.keypoint: Bailable means entitled; non-bailable means the court decides.

body.prompt: Danial's mother is told at the counter that he can come home today if she pays three thousand ringgit. What is that money?
options: A deposit that comes back if he attends every date
A fine for what he is accused of
A payment to the police for letting him out
body.reveal: The third, and the word for it is bail. It secures one thing: that Danial turns up. If you thought fine, you are in very good company.

body.text: Bail is not a fine and it is not a punishment. It is a promise to come back to court, backed by money.
For a bailable offence the accused is entitled to be released on bail. For a non-bailable offence bail is in the discretion of the court.
body.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593), First Schedule and s 388

body.text: Which one applies is looked up rather than argued. The First Schedule to the Code classifies each offence.
A surety, or penjamin, is a person who promises the court that the accused will attend. If the accused disappears, the surety can lose the money.
Bail is set at three thousand ringgit with one surety. Danial's mother signs the bond and deposits the money. If he attends every date, it comes back at the end.
Some Acts carry their own bail rules, and a few shut bail out. Check the Act the charge is brought under, not only the Code.

sections.keypoint: A criminal trial runs in the same order in a small case and a large one.

body.text: A criminal trial has an order, and it is the same order in a small case and a large one.

items: The prosecution calls its witnesses. Each one can be cross-examined by the defence.
The court then decides whether there is a case to answer. If there is not, the accused is acquitted.
If there is, the defence is called. The accused may give evidence or stay silent.
The court gives its decision. If it convicts, it hears mitigation before passing sentence.

body.text: Mitigation is the accused's chance to explain his circumstances before sentence. It is not a denial of guilt.
Dates get adjourned, often. Several mention dates before a trial is normal and is not a sign that something has gone wrong.
A mention date is a short hearing to move the case along. Nobody gives evidence at one. It is the day the court fixes the next thing to happen.
If the family cannot pay for a lawyer, ask about legal aid before the next date, not on the morning of it.

sections.keypoint: The problem puts you in the mother's position, not the lawyer's.

body.text: Five cards, then the problem question on remand and bail. It puts you in the position of the mother, not the lawyer.
After that, the lesson on bail and the shape of a criminal trial takes the same ground at a harder level.

lessons.verify: The maximum remand periods under s 117 of the Criminal Procedure Code are graduated by the sentence the offence carries and have been amended — check the current text. Bail classification comes from the First Schedule, and a special Act may displace it, so check the Act the charge is brought under. quiz.q: Who can allow the police to hold a person beyond twenty-four hours?
options: The investigating officer
The Public Prosecutor
The officer in charge of the station
A Magistrate, by a remand order
quiz.why: Remand is a judicial decision under s 117. The police ask; the Magistrate decides.
quiz.source: Criminal Procedure Code s 117

quiz.q: What is the question at a remand hearing?
options: Whether the accused is guilty
Whether bail should be granted
Whether the charge is properly drafted
Whether further detention is needed for the investigation
quiz.why: Guilt is not in issue yet. Arguing innocence there wastes the one argument you have.
quiz.source: Criminal Procedure Code s 117

quiz.q: What must a charge tell the accused?
options: The likely sentence
The evidence the prosecution holds
The names of the witnesses
The offence, with enough detail of time, place and person
quiz.why: A person cannot answer a case he has not been told. A vague charge is one to raise at once.
quiz.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593); the provisions on the form of a charge

quiz.q: What does claiming trial mean?
options: Asking for a faster hearing
Asking to be tried in a higher court
Admitting the facts but disputing the sentence
Pleading not guilty, so the prosecution must prove the charge
quiz.why: It is the ordinary way a not guilty plea is described in a Malaysian court.
quiz.source: Standard Malaysian court practice; claiming trial is a plea of not guilty

quiz.q: What is a surety promising?
options: That the accused is innocent
To pay any fine the court imposes
That the accused will attend court, with money at risk if he does not
To keep the accused at home
quiz.why: Bail secures attendance. The surety's money is the security, and it comes back if the dates are kept.
quiz.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593); the bail and bond provisions

quiz.q: When is bail a matter of right rather than of discretion?
options: When the accused has no record
When the accused is under twenty-one
When the police do not object
When the offence is classified as bailable
quiz.why: The First Schedule does the classifying. Non-bailable means the court has a discretion, not that bail is impossible.
quiz.source: Criminal Procedure Code, First Schedule; ss 387 and 388

lessons.title: Who owns this land, and how would you know
lessons.summary: The register decides ownership in Malaysia. A land search is how an ordinary person reads it, and occupation is not the same thing as title.

sections.keypoint: Ask who owns a piece of land and most people answer with a family story.

body.text: Ask who owns a piece of land and most people answer with a story. Grandfather cleared it. The family has been there since before Merdeka.

body.prompt: Mak Cik Zainab's family has farmed the same lot for forty years. Her father cleared it, and died fifteen years ago. Nobody has been to the land office since. Who owns it today?
options: Her father, because his name is still on the register
Mak Cik Zainab and her brothers and sisters
Nobody, until a court is asked to decide
body.reveal: Her father. A man fifteen years dead is still, on paper, the owner. That is the ordinary position of a lot of family land here. If you picked the first answer you reasoned the way the village does. The law reasons from one page instead.

body.text: Malaysian land law does not answer with a story. It answers with a register, and the register is kept at the land office.

sections.keypoint: Under the Code you own land by being registered — the register is the title, not a record of it.

body.text: Every piece of registered land in Malaysia has a page in a State register. The person named on that page is the proprietor.
Under the National Land Code a person becomes the owner of land by being registered as proprietor. The register is the title, not merely evidence of it.
This arrangement is called the Torrens system. The name matters less than the habit it should give you. Before you believe anything about land, look at the register.
Mak Cik Zainab's family has farmed a lot in Kuala Selangor for forty years. The register still shows her late father as proprietor. In law the family are not the owners, whatever the village knows.

sections.keypoint: Anyone may order an official search at the district land office; you do not need a lawyer.
sections.h: How to read a land search

body.text: You do not need a lawyer to find out who owns land. Anyone may apply at the district land office for an official search of a lot.
You need the lot number and the mukim or district. The fee is small and the answer comes back on a page or two.

items: The registered proprietor, with an identity card or company number.
The lot number, the area, and the tenure — held for ever, or for a term of years.
The category of land use: agriculture, building or industry.
Any restriction in interest, which is a condition requiring State consent before a sale or a charge.
Anything registered against the land: a charge to a bank, a lease, or a caveat.

body.text: The certificate the family keeps in a biscuit tin is the issue document of title, often called the geran. It is a copy of the register page, not the ownership itself.
A search shows one day only. In a purchase a fresh search is done again just before the transfer is handed in for registration.

sections.keypoint: Long occupation does not turn an occupier into an owner of registered land.
sections.h: Living on land you do not own

body.text: Many Malaysians occupy land they hold no title to. Occupation and ownership are different things, and the Code keeps them apart.

items: A temporary occupation licence, or TOL, is yearly permission to occupy State land. It is permission, not ownership, and it can end.
A tenant rents. The landlord's name stays on the register throughout.
A family arrangement: one child lives on the land while the title stays in a parent's name.

body.text: Long occupation does not by itself give title to registered land under the National Land Code. Time alone does not turn an occupier into an owner.
This surprises people who have heard of squatter's rights in English law. That doctrine does not run against registered land here. The register decides.

Some titles carry a further limit. Malay reserved land can only be dealt with within a restricted class of buyers, under State law. Sabah and Sarawak have their own land legislation, so do not carry this lesson straight across.

body.title: Occupying and owning are different things

items: A TOL is yearly permission to occupy State land. Permission, not ownership.
A tenant rents. The landlord's name stays on the register throughout.
A family arrangement: one child lives there, the title stays in a parent's name.
Long occupation does not by itself give title to registered land.
The register names the proprietor, and the register is the title.
Ownership comes from registration under the National Land Code.
Time alone does not turn an occupier into an owner.
Squatter's rights from English law do not run against registered land here.

sections.keypoint: Signing is not owning: a dealing takes effect on registration, and until then you have contract rights.

body.text: Devi agrees to buy a terrace house in Klang. She signs the sale and purchase agreement and pays the deposit. She has not become the owner.
A dealing in registered land takes effect only when it is registered. Until then the buyer has rights under the contract, not title.
The gap between signing and registration can run for months. Almost everything that goes wrong in a land dispute happens inside that gap.

body.title: Where the danger sits in a purchase
body.caption: The gap can run for months. Almost everything that goes wrong in a land dispute happens inside it, which is why a fresh search is done just before the transfer goes in.
body.alt: Three stages. Devi signs the sale and purchase agreement and pays the deposit, which gives her rights under the contract but not title. Then a gap of months while the transfer is prepared and lodged. Then registration, at which point she becomes the proprietor.

steps.label: Sign, and pay the deposit
steps.note: rights under the contract, not title

steps.label: The gap
steps.note: often months — this is where disputes live

sections.keypoint: If there is land in your family, get the lot number and order a search.

body.text: Five cards. Then, if there is any land in your family, do the real thing. Get the lot number and order a search.
The lesson on title by registration takes the same idea further, into what happens when a registration was obtained by fraud.

quiz.q: Who is the owner of registered land in Malaysia?
options: The person registered as proprietor
The person who has occupied it longest
The person holding the title document
The person who paid for it
quiz.why: The register is the title. Keeping the geran in a drawer is not ownership.
quiz.source: National Land Code (Act 828); title is by registration

quiz.q: What is the geran, the issue document of title?
options: A copy of the register page, held by the proprietor
The contract of sale
The ownership itself
A licence to occupy State land
quiz.why: It is a copy. What settles ownership is the register at the land office.
quiz.source: National Land Code (Act 828); the issue document of title is a copy of the register

quiz.q: What does a restriction in interest on a title mean?
options: The land cannot be dealt with at all
The land is reserved for agriculture
State consent is needed before the land is sold or charged
The proprietor is under eighteen
quiz.why: It is a condition written on the title. Missing it is a common way for a sale to stall.
quiz.source: National Land Code (Act 828); restrictions in interest endorsed on the title

quiz.q: A family has farmed land for forty years with no title in their name. What do they own?
options: The land, by long use
A half share of the land
Nothing in law, unless the register says otherwise
A licence to remain
quiz.why: Long occupation gives no title against the register under the Code.
quiz.source: National Land Code (Act 828); long occupation gives no title against the register

quiz.q: Devi signs a sale and purchase agreement and pays her deposit. What does she have?
options: Title to the land
A registered charge
A caveat over the land
Rights under the contract, but not title
quiz.why: A dealing takes effect on registration, and the gap before it is where the risk sits.
quiz.source: National Land Code (Act 828); a dealing takes effect on registration

lessons.title: The four papers behind a piece of land
lessons.summary: Transfer, charge, caveat, and the grandfather whose name is still on the title — what each document does, and why speed matters when a signature was forged.

sections.keypoint: Most land arguments are arguments about four documents.

body.text: Land arguments are usually arguments about four documents. A transfer, a charge, a caveat, and the paper that moves land on when somebody has died.
Each does one job. Learn what each one does, and most land problems become readable without a textbook.

body.caption: Each does one job. Learn what each one does, and most land problems become readable without a textbook.
rows: Transfer
Changes the registered owner. The buyer's name replaces the seller's.
Charge
What a bank gets over the land when it lends against it.
Caveat
A stop sign on the register.
The paper for a dead owner
Moves the land on when the owner has died.

sections.keypoint: A transfer passes ownership when it is registered, not when it is signed.

body.text: A sale ends with a transfer form signed by the seller and handed in at the land office. The office registers it, and the buyer's name replaces the seller's.
A transfer of registered land passes ownership when it is registered, not when it is signed.
Devi's transfer is handed in on a Monday and registered a fortnight later. She became the owner on the day of registration, not on the day she paid.
Stamp duty is paid before registration. Where the title carries a restriction in interest, State consent has to come first.

sections.keypoint: A charge is security for a debt — and Malaysian law says charge, not mortgage.

body.text: When a bank lends against land, it does not take ownership. It takes a registered security called a charge.
A charge is registered against the land as security for a debt. Malaysian law says charge, not mortgage.
The borrower stays the registered proprietor. The bank appears on the register as chargee, which is a different thing.
If the borrower defaults, the bank serves a notice. If the default is not put right, it applies for an order for sale.
The bank cannot simply take the house and move in. It has to go through the order for sale process, and the borrower can be heard in it.

sections.keypoint: A caveat is the stop sign: it freezes dealings while a claim is sorted out.

body.text: A caveat is a note entered on the register that blocks further dealings while it stands. It is the quickest protection an ordinary person has.
A private caveat may be entered by a person claiming title to the land, or a registrable interest in it, or a beneficial entitlement under a trust affecting it.
A caveat does not give you the land. It buys time by stopping anybody else being registered until the claim is sorted out.
Devi hears that her seller is trying to sell the same house to somebody else. She lodges a private caveat that afternoon. The second sale cannot be registered while it stands.
A caveat lodged without a proper claim is not free. A person who suffers loss because of it can claim compensation from the caveator.

sections.keypoint: Land in a dead person's name moves only when the distribution is registered.

body.text: This is the most common land problem in Malaysian families. It is a paperwork problem rather than a fight.
Land does not pass to the children by itself. The register keeps showing the dead person until the estate is distributed and that distribution is registered.

items: A small estate is dealt with at the Land Office, in a distribution hearing the family attends.
Where there is a will, or the estate is larger, the matter goes to court for a grant.
The order or grant is then registered against the title, and only then does the register change.

body.text: Land registered in a dead person's name moves on only when the distribution of the estate is registered against the title.
body.source: National Land Code (Act 828); Small Estates (Distribution) Act 1955

body.text: Delay is expensive. After two generations the heirs have multiplied, some have moved away, and some have died in turn. The cheapest time to do this is now.

sections.keypoint: Section 340 protects a registered title, and lists the exceptions — fraud, forgery, a void instrument.
sections.h: When a signature is not real

body.text: Sometimes a name reached the register through a forged transfer. The Code does not simply shrug at that.
A registered title is indefeasible, but s 340 sets out exceptions. Registration obtained by fraud, by forgery, or by a void instrument may be set aside.
The Federal Court in Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San restored the deferred position. The forger's transferee can be unwound. A later buyer in good faith, for value, is protected.
That is why speed matters. Once the land has moved on to an innocent buyer, the person who lost it may be left suing for money rather than getting the land back.

quiz.q: When does a buyer become the registered owner?
options: When the agreement is signed
When the price is paid in full
When the transfer is registered
When the keys are handed over
quiz.why: Registration is the moment. Everything before it is contract.
quiz.source: National Land Code (Act 828); a transfer takes effect on registration

quiz.q: What does a bank get when it lends against land?
options: Ownership of the land
A registered charge, as security for the debt
A caveat over the land
A lease of the land
quiz.why: Malaysian law says charge, not mortgage, and the borrower stays the proprietor.
quiz.source: National Land Code (Act 828); the charge provisions

quiz.q: What does a private caveat do?
options: It blocks further dealings from being registered
It transfers the land to the caveator
It cancels the seller's title
It creates a charge over the land
quiz.why: It buys time; it gives no interest. Lodging one without a proper claim can cost compensation.
quiz.source: National Land Code (Act 828); the caveat provisions

quiz.q: A father dies with land in his name. What happens to the register?
options: It passes to the eldest child at once
It passes to the widow at once
It goes back to the State
Nothing, until the estate is distributed and the distribution registered
quiz.why: Land does not move by itself. The distribution has to be obtained and then registered.
quiz.source: Small Estates (Distribution) Act 1955; National Land Code (Act 828)

quiz.q: Where is a small estate usually distributed?
options: At the Land Office, in a distribution hearing
At the Sessions Court
At the National Registration Department
At the State Secretary's office
quiz.why: Small estates go through the Land Office. Larger ones, or those with a will, go to court.
quiz.source: Small Estates (Distribution) Act 1955

quiz.q: A transfer was forged. Is the person registered under it safe?
options: Yes, because the register is always conclusive
Yes, if a lawyer witnessed the signature
No — forgery is one of the exceptions in s 340
Only if the true owner objects within a year
quiz.why: The exceptions are listed. It is the later innocent buyer for value who is protected, which is why speed matters.
quiz.source: National Land Code s 340; Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010] 2 MLJ 1 (FC)

lessons.plateCaption: Four papers, four jobs. Knowing which one is in front of you answers most questions before any law is applied.

lessons.title: Leases and tenancies, and the line registration draws
lessons.summary: A lease of registered land is a dealing, so it lives on the register and binds whoever buys the land. A short tenancy is exempt from registration, which changes what a buyer of that land ever sees.

sections.keypoint: Two shoplots, two rent agreements, and the Code files them in completely different places.
sections.h: Two shoplots on the same street

body.text: Puan Halimah rents her shoplot in Ipoh to Encik Kamal. The term is five years. The rent is RM2,400 a month.
Two doors down, Encik Suresh rents an identical shoplot to a baker. That term is two years, at the same rent.
Same street. Same building. Same money. The Code treats the two agreements as different animals.

body.prompt: A buyer purchases both shoplots. She orders a land search on each title. Which of the two rent agreements is she likely to see on the register?
options: Kamal's five-year agreement
Both, because both are rent agreements
Suresh's two-year agreement
body.reveal: The longer one. A lease of registered land is a dealing, so it is registered and it shows. A short tenancy is exempt from registration, so the register may say nothing about it at all. That gap is the whole of this lesson.

sections.keypoint: Length of term decides everything: a lease is registered, and a short tenancy cannot be.
sections.h: Where the Code draws the line

body.text: The Code does not ask what the parties called their document. It asks how long the term is.
Above a short threshold the arrangement is a lease. A lease is one of the dealings the Code allows, and it takes effect on registration.

A tenancy for a term not exceeding three years is a tenancy exempt from registration under the National Land Code, and it cannot be registered. An arrangement granting possession for a longer term must be created as a registered lease.
body.source: National Land Code, the provisions on leases and on tenancies exempt from registration. No section number is stated here on purpose.

body.caption: Lease and short tenancy compared, on the points that decide a real dispute
rows: How long is the term?
Longer than the short statutory threshold
Not exceeding three years
Does it go on the register?
Yes, as a registrable dealing
No, it cannot be registered
When does it take effect?
On registration
On the agreement, by contract
Can a buyer of the land see it?
Yes, on a land search
Only from an endorsement, or from the tenant being there
body.alt: A table comparing a registered lease with a short tenancy. A lease runs longer than the statutory threshold. It is a registrable dealing, it takes effect on registration, and it shows on a land search. A short tenancy runs for not more than three years and cannot be registered. It takes effect by contract. A buyer sees it only from an endorsement, or from the tenant being visibly there.

body.text: The three-year line is the one figure in this lesson. Confirm it in the current Code before you rely on it. Note too that the Code caps how long a lease may run.
That cap is not the same for the whole of a lot and for part of one. This lesson does not give those figures. Look them up.

sections.keypoint: A registered lease is an interest in the land itself; a short tenancy leans on contract and on being seen.

body.text: Registration is not paperwork for its own sake. It changes what the tenant owns.

Section 340(1) protects the title or interest of any person for the time being registered as proprietor, and of any person in whose name a lease, charge or easement is registered. A registered lease is therefore indefeasible on the same terms as a registered title.
So Kamal holds an interest in the land itself. If Halimah sells the shoplot, the buyer takes it with Kamal's lease already on the register.
Suresh's baker is weaker. The tenancy is a contract with Suresh, and it cannot be put on the register at all.
The Code answers that with an endorsement. A tenancy exempt from registration can be noted on the register, so a buyer searching the title sees it.
A tenant who does nothing is relying on two things. One is the contract. The other is that a careful buyer will notice somebody trading from the shop and ask why.
Raise this before signing, not after. Ask whether the tenancy will be endorsed, and ask who pays for that.

sections.keypoint: A landlord who wants possession back goes to court; changing the locks is not a remedy.

body.text: A lease or tenancy ends in three ordinary ways. The term runs out, the parties agree to end it, or the tenant breaks a term.

items: **The term runs out.** Nothing more is needed, though a registered lease still has to come off the register.
**Surrender.** The parties agree to end it early, and a registered lease is again dealt with on the register.
**Forfeiture for breach.** The landlord serves notice of the breach first, and gives a chance to put it right.

body.text: What a landlord may not do is take the shop back by hand. That is the rule that surprises people most.
A person in possession of immovable property may not be dispossessed except by due process of law. Self-help recovery of possession is not permitted, and possession is recovered through the court.
body.source: Specific Relief Act 1950, the provisions on recovery of possession. No section number is stated here on purpose.

body.text: Changing the locks, cutting the water, or carting out the tenant's stock is unlawful. It also hands the tenant a claim, which is the opposite of what the landlord wanted.

body.q: Kamal stops paying rent. Halimah changes the locks on the shoplot early one Sunday. Where does that leave her?
options: She has lawfully forfeited the lease, because the rent was unpaid
She has acted unlawfully, and Kamal may sue to be let back in
She is safe, because the lease was registered in Kamal's name
body.why: Unpaid rent may well justify forfeiture. It does not justify taking possession by hand. Possession is recovered through the court, and self-help gives Kamal a claim of his own. Notice how the two questions separate. Whether Halimah has a right, and how she may enforce it, are not the same question.

lessons.source: National Land Code, the provisions on leases, on tenancies exempt from registration and on endorsement, together with s 340(1) on indefeasibility; Specific Relief Act 1950 on recovery of possession.

lessons.title: Owning land with other people
lessons.summary: Two or more people on one title hold undivided shares, and an undivided share is not a piece of ground. Nothing in the Code lets one of them fence off a corner and call it theirs.

sections.keypoint: Three siblings, one lot in Kuala Pilah, and a brother who wants to build on his third.

body.text: Suriani, Faizal and Nurul are on one title in Kuala Pilah. The lot is two acres. It came to them from their late father's estate.
The register shows each of them with an undivided one-third share.
Faizal wants to build a house at the back of the lot. He says the back third is his.

body.prompt: Faizal fences off the back third of the lot and starts building. Is he entitled to?
options: Yes, because he owns a third of the land
Only if his share is the largest of the three
No, because his third is a share of the whole lot and not a part of the ground
body.reveal: His share is a fraction of the whole, not a marked-out piece. Until the land is partitioned, no co-proprietor can point at any part of the ground and call it theirs. If you thought a third meant a third of the field, that is the instinct the word undivided exists to correct.

sections.keypoint: Each share is a fraction of the whole lot, and a dead co-proprietor's share falls into the estate.

body.text: The word to hold on to is undivided. A share is a fraction of the entire lot, from the front fence to the back.

Where land is held under the National Land Code by two or more persons, they hold as co-proprietors in undivided shares. No co-proprietor is entitled to any defined part of the land, and each is entitled to possession of the whole.
body.source: National Land Code, the provisions on co-proprietorship. No section number is stated here on purpose.

body.text: There is a second consequence, and it catches people trained on English land law.
The Code does not provide for a right of survivorship between co-proprietors. On the death of a co-proprietor, the share forms part of that person's estate and passes under it.
body.source: National Land Code, the provisions on co-proprietorship, read with the law on the distribution of estates. No section number is stated here on purpose.

body.text: So Nurul's third does not fall to her brother and sister when she dies. It goes into her estate, and her own heirs take it.

body.caption: What each co-proprietor has, and what none of them has
rows: A defined piece of the ground
No. Shares are undivided until the lot is partitioned.
A right to be on the land
Yes. Each co-proprietor may possess the whole of it.
A right to keep the others out
No. Possession of the whole belongs to all of them.
A share that passes on death
Yes, through the estate. There is no survivorship.
body.alt: A table of four claims. A defined piece of ground: no, shares are undivided until partition. A right to be on the land: yes, each co-proprietor may possess the whole. A right to keep the others out: no, they all possess the whole. A share that passes on death: yes, through the estate, because there is no survivorship.

sections.keypoint: You may sell or charge your own share alone; the whole lot needs every co-proprietor.
sections.h: What one co-proprietor may do alone

body.text: A share is property. Faizal can sell his third, and a bank can take a charge over it.

items: **Your own share.** You may transfer it, or charge it, without asking the others.
**The whole lot.** A transfer, lease or charge of the whole needs all the co-proprietors.
**The ground itself.** Nobody may fence a part off, or shut the others out of it.
**Rent collected.** A co-proprietor who takes the whole rent can be made to account to the rest.

body.text: Selling a share is lawful and still hard. Few buyers want a one-third share of a lot with two strangers on the title, and the price shows it.
There is a quieter risk. A share can be charged, and a charge on one share can end in an order for sale of that share.
The others can protect their position on the register instead of arguing later.
A private caveat may be entered by a person claiming title to the land, or claiming any registrable interest in it, or claiming to be beneficially entitled under any trust affecting it.
That matters most before an estate is distributed. An heir is not yet on the register, and a caveat is a common way to hold the claim in place.
Whether an heir of an undistributed estate has a caveatable interest has been fought over more than once. Check the current position before you advise anyone to lodge one.

sections.keypoint: Partition turns shares into separate titles; where it cannot be done, the answer is a sale.

body.text: The clean answer to Faizal's problem is partition. Partition ends co-proprietorship by cutting the lot into separate titles.
After partition each of them holds a lot of their own, with a title of their own. Only then can Faizal build at the back.

items: Partition is applied for at the land office, under the procedure the Code lays down.
Each resulting lot has to satisfy the Code's requirements, including any minimum area.
Whose consent is needed, and when partition may be refused, are set out in the Code.
Where partition is not practicable, the route is a sale of the whole land instead.

body.text: Do not leave this to the next generation. Three co-proprietors become nine, then twenty, and every one of them has to be found and has to sign.

body.q: Suriani, Faizal and Nurul cannot agree. Faizal wants a title of his own over the back of the lot. What does he need?
options: Partition of the lot, so that a separate title issues
A private caveat over the back third
Nothing, because a one-third share already gives him a third of the ground
body.why: A caveat only freezes the register, and it hands over no piece of ground. His share stays undivided until the lot is partitioned. Partition is the procedure that turns a share of the whole into a lot of his own, and it is applied for at the land office.

lessons.title: Strata title, and what you own in a condominium
lessons.summary: A condominium buyer owns a parcel and an undivided share of the common property, measured in share units. Almost every argument in a strata building starts at that one division.

sections.keypoint: Puan Meera has keys, a car park bay and a lift she uses daily, and she does not own all three.

body.text: Puan Meera buys a condominium unit in Cheras for RM480,000. She gets keys to unit B-12-3 and a car park bay downstairs.
She uses the lift every day and the pool on Sundays. The corridor outside her door is swept by somebody she has never met.

body.prompt: Meera owns unit B-12-3. Which of these does she own outright, on her own?
options: The unit only, plus an undivided share of everything that is shared
The unit, the corridor and her share of the lift
The unit and the car park, but not the corridor
body.reveal: The parcel is hers. Everything shared is common property, and she holds an undivided share of it with every other owner. The car park is usually an accessory parcel, tied to her unit and not sellable apart from it. Almost every strata argument begins at that line.

sections.keypoint: Parcels and common property split the building; share units then measure money and votes.

body.text: A strata scheme divides one building on one lot into many titles. The division is done by survey and recorded in a strata plan.

Under the Strata Titles Act 1985 a building is divided into parcels and common property. A parcel proprietor holds a strata title to the parcel, together with an undivided share in the common property. The size of that share is expressed in share units.
body.source: Strata Titles Act 1985. No section number is stated here on purpose.

body.caption: The vocabulary of a strata scheme, and what each word actually owns
rows: Parcel
The unit itself. Meera holds a strata title to it.
Common property
Everything outside the parcels: corridors, lifts, roof, pool, drains.
Accessory parcel
A car park or store tied to a parcel. It cannot be sold on its own.
Share unit
The measure of a parcel's share, its charges and its vote.
Management corporation
The body of all parcel proprietors, which holds the common property.
body.alt: Five strata words. A parcel is the unit itself, held under a strata title. Common property is everything outside the parcels, such as corridors, lifts, roof, pool and drains. An accessory parcel is a car park or store tied to a parcel and not sellable on its own. A share unit measures a parcel's share, its charges and its vote. The management corporation is the body of all proprietors, and it holds the common property.

body.text: Share units do more work than anything else in the scheme. They set what Meera pays each month, and how much her vote is worth.
Read the schedule of share units before buying. A large parcel carries more share units, so it carries a larger share of every bill the building runs up.

sections.keypoint: Management passes from developer to joint management body to management corporation, in that order.

body.text: Somebody has to sweep the corridor and service the lift. Malaysian law hands that job on in stages.

items: **The developer** manages first, from vacant possession until a joint management body is formed.
**The joint management body** is formed at a meeting of buyers, and runs the building before strata titles issue.
**The management corporation** comes into being once strata titles issue, and takes over at the first annual general meeting.

body.text: The Strata Management Act 2013 governs the management of stratified property. It covers the maintenance account and the sinking fund, the by-laws, and the recovery of charges. Contributions are payable in proportion to the share units of each parcel.
body.source: Strata Management Act 2013. No section number is stated here on purpose.

body.text: Two funds matter. The maintenance account pays the day-to-day bills. The sinking fund pays for the big repairs that come later.
Arrears are not a private matter between one owner and the management. The Act gives the management body ways to recover them, and an owner in arrears can lose the right to vote.
By-laws bind everyone in the building. Some of them are prescribed by the Act, and the owners may add their own by a proper resolution.

sections.keypoint: Late strata titles leave a buyer with contract rights only, sometimes for years.

body.text: Two problems come up more than any others. Charges go unpaid, and strata titles are late.
The second one bites hardest. A buyer can take vacant possession years before a strata title issues for the parcel.
Until then Meera is not the registered proprietor of anything. She holds rights under her sale and purchase agreement, against the developer.
Once the strata title issues and is registered in her name, she is a registered proprietor. Section 340 then protects her parcel as it protects any other registered title.
The Strata Management Tribunal hears many strata disputes cheaply, and it is meant to be used without a lawyer. It has a monetary limit, and some disputes belong in court instead.

body.q: Meera took vacant possession two years ago. No strata title has issued yet. What does she hold?
options: A registered title to the parcel
Rights under her agreement with the developer, but no registered title
An undivided share of the master title, registered in her name
body.why: Registration is what makes a proprietor, and there is no strata title to register yet. Until it issues she holds contractual rights against the developer. This is the same gap you met between signing and registration in an ordinary sale, stretched out over years.

lessons.source: Strata Titles Act 1985; Strata Management Act 2013; National Land Code, s 340 on indefeasibility and the parts on subdivision of buildings.

lessons.title: When the State takes your land
lessons.summary: The State can take registered land compulsorily, and an indefeasible title is no answer to it. What an owner can usually fight about is not the taking but the money.

sections.keypoint: A clean title, no charge, no caveat, and a notice on the fence that ends the argument.

body.text: Encik Ganesan's family has held a lot in Seberang Perai for thirty years. The register is clean. There is no charge and no caveat.
One morning a notice is nailed to the fence. The land is wanted for a road.

body.prompt: Ganesan is the registered proprietor, and his title is indefeasible. Does that stop the State taking the land?
options: No, because compulsory acquisition works whatever the register says
Yes, because an indefeasible title cannot be taken away
Only if he lodges a caveat quickly enough
body.reveal: Indefeasibility protects you against other people. It is no answer to the State using a statutory power to acquire. What the law gives Ganesan instead is process and compensation. If you assumed a clean title was a shield, this is the lesson that fixes that.

sections.keypoint: The State Authority acquires, and the Constitution demands law and adequate compensation.
sections.h: The power, and what it is for

body.text: Land is a State matter. It is the State Authority, not the Federal Government, that acquires land in a State.

Land may be compulsorily acquired by the State Authority under the Land Acquisition Act 1960 for the purposes that Act names. Those include a public purpose, and a purpose the State Authority is satisfied is beneficial to the economic development of the country.
body.source: Land Acquisition Act 1960. No section number is stated here on purpose.

body.text: The Federal Constitution sits above the Act. It forbids deprivation of property except in accordance with law, and it requires adequate compensation.
No person shall be deprived of property save in accordance with law, and no law shall provide for the compulsory acquisition or use of property without adequate compensation.
body.source: Federal Constitution, the guarantee on deprivation of property. No article number is stated here on purpose.

body.text: The economic development purpose is the controversial one. Land can be taken from a family and end up in the hands of a company, and the Act permits that on its own terms.
Notice what the Constitution does and does not do. It insists on law, and on adequate compensation. It does not give you a right to keep the land.

sections.keypoint: Notification, gazetted declaration, enquiry, award, possession, and the declaration is hard to attack.

body.text: The Act runs in a fixed order. Knowing the order tells you where you still have something worth saying.

body.caption: The stages of a compulsory acquisition, and what happens at each one
rows: Preliminary notification
The State signals that land in the area may be needed. Surveys may follow.
Declaration in the Gazette
The State declares that the land is needed for the stated purpose.
Enquiry
The Land Administrator hears evidence on value and on who is entitled.
Award
Compensation is awarded, and the award is served on the persons interested.
Possession and vesting
The State takes possession, and the land vests in the State Authority.
body.alt: Five stages of a compulsory acquisition. First a preliminary notification that land in an area may be needed, which surveys may follow. Then a declaration in the State Gazette that the land is needed for the stated purpose. Then an enquiry before the Land Administrator into value and entitlement. Then an award of compensation, served on the persons interested. Last, possession is taken and the land vests in the State Authority.

body.text: A declaration published in the Gazette is treated by the Act as conclusive evidence that the land is needed for the purpose stated in it.
body.source: Land Acquisition Act 1960. No section number is stated here on purpose.

body.text: Read that rule twice. It is why arguing that the road is unnecessary almost never works.
Attend the enquiry, and bring evidence of value. A person who ignores the enquiry throws away the cheapest chance to be heard about money.
The people paid are the persons interested, and that is wider than the proprietor. A registered chargee or lessee has a claim on the compensation too.

sections.keypoint: Market value at the date of the declaration, plus named heads, then a reference to the High Court.
sections.h: Compensation, and how to fight about it

body.text: Compensation is built on market value, taken at the date of the declaration. What the land is worth years later is not the question.

items: **Market value** of the land at the date of the declaration in the Gazette.
**Severance**, where taking part of a lot damages the value of the rest.
**Injurious affection**, where the works themselves harm the land left behind.
**Removal or relocation costs**, where the taking forces a move.
**Not** an extra allowance simply because the taking was compulsory.

body.text: One more exclusion is worth remembering. A rise in value caused by the scheme itself is not paid for.
If the award is too low, the owner objects and asks for a reference to the High Court. The judge hears it sitting with assessors who know land values.

body.q: Ganesan thinks the award for his lot is far too low. What is his route?
options: An objection at the enquiry, then a reference to the High Court on the amount
Judicial review of the declaration, on the ground that the road is unnecessary
A private caveat, to stop the land vesting in the State
body.why: The declaration is treated as conclusive that the land is needed, so attacking the purpose almost never works. The amount is a different question, and the Act gives a route for it. Object at the enquiry, then ask for a reference heard by a judge sitting with assessors. A caveat does nothing against a statutory power.

lessons.source: Land Acquisition Act 1960; the Federal Constitution's guarantee against deprivation of property without adequate compensation; National Land Code, on registered title generally.

lessons.title: Search, seizure, and what the police may take
lessons.summary: A search of your shop, your phone or your body is a use of power, and the Criminal Procedure Code decides when that power exists. What you ask for at the door, and what you write down, matters more than anything you argue there.

sections.keypoint: Consent and a legal power are different things, and the officer at your door may be relying on either one.
sections.h: Four officers at the shop door

body.text: Encik Rajan repairs phones in a shop lot in Seremban. At ten in the morning four police officers walk in. They ask to look at the stockroom at the back.
Rajan has two questions and no time to think. Must he let them in? And what happens to his stock if they take it?
Start with the difference between asking and having a power. An officer who asks, and is told yes, is searching with your consent.
An officer with a power does not need your yes. Which of the two is happening changes what you can complain about afterwards.

body.prompt: The officers have no warrant. Rajan says nothing and steps aside to let them past. What has he done?
options: Probably consented, because stepping aside reads as agreement
Refused, because silence can never be agreement
Nothing at all, because only a written refusal counts in law
body.reveal: Silence and a step back read as agreement to almost everyone in the room. If you mean to object, say the words out loud, and ask someone to note the time you said them. Objecting in words is not obstruction, and it is the only way to keep the point alive.

body.text: Consent given at the door is very hard to argue about months later. If you agree, say so plainly. If you do not agree, say that plainly too, and then stand aside.

sections.keypoint: Some searches need a court's written order and some do not, and the Code does not answer the same way for every situation.
sections.h: A warrant, or a power that needs none

body.text: A search warrant is a written order from a court. It names the place that may be searched and says what is being looked for.
The Code also gives the police powers to search without a warrant. Those powers arise in defined situations, and each one carries its own conditions.

A search warrant is issued by a court and authorises a named search. The Criminal Procedure Code also provides for search without a warrant in defined circumstances, and each of those powers has its own conditions attached to it.
body.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593), the provisions on search warrants and on search without a warrant

body.text: The power most people meet is the search of a person who has just been arrested. An arrested person may be searched, and what is found may be taken.
So ask two things at the door, and ask them calmly. Is there a warrant? If not, what power is being used?

items: Ask whether the officers have a warrant, and ask to read it before they start.
If there is one, note what place it covers and what it says is being looked for.
If there is none, ask what power is being used, and write down the answer given.
Note the time the search started and the time it finished.

body.text: Do not tear up a warrant, block a doorway, or hide anything. Obstruction is an offence of its own. Objecting in words costs you nothing, and obstruction costs you a charge.

sections.keypoint: Seized things have to be listed, and that list is the document you will need many months later.
sections.h: What may be taken, and the list

body.text: Seizure is taking a thing away. It is not the same act as searching, and it is the part that closes a small business.
Property seized must be listed, and the Criminal Procedure Code governs how seized property is then held, returned or disposed of, including by an order of the court.
body.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593), the provisions on the list of things seized and on the disposal of property

body.text: Rajan's stockroom holds forty phones worth about RM30,000. Six are taken away. He should ask for a written list, with the model and serial number of each one.

body.caption: What to record on the day of a search
rows: The names or numbers of the officers, and their station
You will need to say who was there, and memory of a bad morning fades
Whether there was a warrant, and what it covered
A search that went wider than the warrant is a point worth taking
Everything taken, with serial numbers
Getting property back turns on identifying the exact thing
The time the search began and ended
Times anchor every other account of what happened
body.alt: Four things to record on the day of a search, each with the reason it matters later. The officers present and their station: you will need to say who was there. Whether there was a warrant and what it covered: a search that went wider is a point worth taking. Everything taken, with serial numbers: getting property back turns on identifying the exact thing. The times the search began and ended: times anchor every other account.

body.text: Getting property back is its own application, made to a court. Start it early, and start it with the list in your hand.

sections.keypoint: An unlawful search does not usually make the thing found inadmissible, and the remedy for it lies somewhere else.

body.text: Suppose the search was unlawful. Many people assume that whatever was found cannot then be used against them. That is not the Malaysian position.
Evidence may be given of the existence of every fact in issue and of such other facts as are declared to be relevant. The Evidence Act works through relevance.
Relevance is the gate the Act uses. How a thing came to be found is a different question from whether it is relevant.
So unlawfully obtained evidence is not automatically shut out here. Courts have been asked to exclude it, and that argument is live rather than settled.
None of that makes an unlawful search harmless. It may support a complaint, a civil claim, or an attack on the weight of what was found. It is simply not a reliable route to exclusion.

body.q: The officers searched Rajan's stockroom with no warrant and no power to do so. They found stolen phones. What follows?
options: The phones are likely to be admissible, and the unlawfulness is fought on other ground
The charge against Rajan must be withdrawn
The phones cannot be used in evidence at all
body.why: Malaysian courts have not treated legality and relevance as the same question. The unlawfulness may found a complaint or a civil claim, and it may be used on weight. Exclusion is not the ordinary consequence, so never build a defence on it alone.

body.text: Ask the harder question instead. Can the prosecution prove that these are the stolen phones, and that Rajan knew what they were?

lessons.title: Appeal, revision, and who may ask for each
lessons.summary: An appeal belongs to a party, runs on a short clock, and goes to a court fixed by which court decided the case. Revision is the High Court looking at a subordinate court's record, and nobody has a right to it.

sections.keypoint: One route belongs to the parties and runs on a clock; the other belongs to the High Court and does not.
sections.h: Two ways to attack a decision

body.text: Puan Kamala was convicted in the Sessions Court in Klang and fined RM5,000. She believes the judge got the law wrong.
At the court counter her son hears two words. Appeal, and revision. They are not two names for the same thing.

items: An appeal is brought by a party. It has a form, a time limit, and a court that must hear it.
A revision is the High Court looking at the record of a court below. Nobody has a right to one.

body.text: The practical difference is control. Kamala can start an appeal herself. A revision is something she can only invite.
Appeals in criminal matters, and the revisionary jurisdiction of the High Court over the subordinate courts, are provided for by the Criminal Procedure Code and by the Courts of Judicature Act 1964.
body.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593); Courts of Judicature Act 1964 (Act 91)

body.prompt: Kamala has missed the time limit for an appeal by three weeks. Is there anything left for her?
options: Nothing at all, because the time limit ends the matter
Possibly: the High Court's revisionary power does not run on her deadline
She may simply file late, because criminal time limits are advisory
body.reveal: Revision is the High Court's own power over the record below, so it is not started by her and is not governed by her deadline. But it is no substitute for an appeal, and a court will not welcome it being used as one. Ask, and never plan on it.

sections.keypoint: Both sides may appeal, and a guilty plea narrows what an appeal is allowed to attack.
sections.h: Who may appeal, and against what

body.text: Appeals are not only for the convicted. The prosecution has appeal rights of its own, and people forget that.

items: A convicted person may appeal against the conviction, against the sentence, or against both.
The Public Prosecutor may appeal against an acquittal, and against a sentence thought too light.
A person who pleaded guilty is restricted, and the Code limits what such an appeal may attack.

body.text: That last one catches people every week. Pleading guilty on a Monday and regretting it on a Friday is common. Very little is left to argue.
The Code sets the time for filing an appeal, and it is short. It is counted in days from the decision, not from the day a lawyer was found. Look the period up in the same week.

sections.keypoint: The court above is fixed by the court that decided, and a case begun in a subordinate court has little road left.

body.text: The route upward is not chosen. It is fixed by which court decided the case in the first place.

body.caption: Where a criminal appeal goes, by the court that decided
rows: Magistrates' Court
The High Court
Sessions Court
The High Court
High Court, trying the case itself
The Court of Appeal
Court of Appeal
The Federal Court, where the Act allows it
body.alt: Where a criminal appeal goes, by the court that decided. From the Magistrates' Court, to the High Court. From the Sessions Court, also to the High Court. From the High Court trying a case itself, to the Court of Appeal. From the Court of Appeal, to the Federal Court where the Act allows it.

body.text: A case that started in a subordinate court has already had one appeal by the time the High Court decides it. Going further than that is restricted.
The restriction on a further appeal sits in the Courts of Judicature Act 1964. Read what it allows before you tell anybody the case can go higher.
An appellate court is not limited to yes or no. It may confirm, reverse or vary the decision, and it may order a new trial.

body.q: Kamala was tried in the Sessions Court and then lost her appeal in the High Court. Can she go to the Court of Appeal?
options: Yes, as of right, in the same way as any other appeal
Only if the Courts of Judicature Act allows a further appeal in her situation
No, because the High Court is always the last word
body.why: A second appeal in a case that began below is restricted, and the restriction is statutory. Neither a flat yes nor a flat no is safe. Read the Act before promising a client anything about a further appeal.

sections.keypoint: Revision corrects what is plainly wrong on the record, and it is not a second chance to argue the evidence.
sections.h: Revision, and what it is for

body.text: Revision is supervision. The High Court may call for the record of a subordinate court and satisfy itself that the decision was correct and lawful.
Anyone may bring a matter to the court's attention. A party may write in, and so may the Public Prosecutor. The court may also act on its own.
A Magistrate passes a sentence the law does not allow for that offence. Nobody appealed in time. Revision is how a thing like that gets put right.
Revision is not for re-arguing evidence. It is for what is plainly wrong on the face of the record, such as an illegal sentence or a fundamental irregularity.
If an order in revision might go against a person, that person is heard first. Nobody is made worse off unheard.

lessons.title: Making a witness turn up
lessons.summary: A case is decided on the evidence that reaches the courtroom, not on the evidence that exists somewhere. The Code has two ways of compelling a witness, and the Evidence Act says which questions that witness may still refuse.

sections.keypoint: The best witness in the case is worth nothing to you if she is not in the box on the day.
sections.h: The witness who stops answering the phone

body.text: Cik Suriani runs a salon in Kuantan. She saw the fight outside her shop and told the police everything she saw.
The trial is in six weeks. Suriani has stopped answering her phone. She is frightened of the accused's family.
This is the ordinary problem of criminal practice. The evidence exists. Getting it into the courtroom is a separate job from finding it.
The Code answers that job with a document, and then with an arrest if the document is ignored.

sections.keypoint: A summons orders attendance, and ignoring one can end with the witness herself under arrest.

body.text: A summons to a witness is a court order to attend on a named day. It is served on the person, and the service is recorded.
A court may issue a summons requiring a person to attend and give evidence or produce a document, and may issue a warrant to secure the attendance of a person who fails to obey it.
body.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593), the provisions on securing the attendance of witnesses

body.text: So the ladder has two rungs. The summons is the first one. A warrant for the witness is the second, and it is not the usual first step.

items: Ask the court to issue the summons early, not in the week before trial.
Give the court a real address, and a way of actually reaching the person.
Tell the witness the day, the court and the time. Frightened people miss dates.
If a summons was ignored, tell the court why, and ask for what you actually need.

body.text: Arresting a frightened witness is a poor way to get good evidence. Ask what the fear is first. A different date, a word from the investigating officer, or protection often does far more.

body.prompt: Suriani is served with a summons and still does not come to court. What is the court's first move likely to be?
options: Strike out the prosecution's case for want of evidence
Adjourn, and then consider a warrant to secure her attendance
Convict on the statement she gave the police
body.reveal: Courts want the witness, not a punishment. The usual course is a fresh date, and a warrant only if that fails too. Her police statement is not simply read out in her place, and that is exactly why her attendance matters so much.

sections.keypoint: Attendance can be compelled, but a few questions are protected, and legal privilege belongs to the client.
sections.h: What a witness may still refuse

body.text: A summons compels attendance. It does not compel every answer once the witness is in the box.
The best known protection covers what a client tells a lawyer. It sits in the Evidence Act, and it belongs to the client rather than to the lawyer.

An advocate is not permitted to disclose a communication made to him in the course and for the purpose of his employment as an advocate, except with the client's express consent, and subject to the exceptions the Act itself states.
Read the sections after s 126 along with it. They deal with waiver, with interpreters and clerks, and with confidential communications with a legal adviser.
There is a second protection, and it comes up far more often. A witness need not answer a question whose answer would expose him to a criminal charge.
Do not tell a witness what to say. Explaining the procedure to a nervous witness is proper and kind. Telling her what her evidence should be is neither, and it is an offence.

sections.keypoint: A missing witness can cost you twice: the evidence is gone, and the court may hold the gap against you.
sections.h: When the witness never comes at all

body.text: Sometimes a witness simply cannot be found. The case then runs on what is left, and two rules of evidence start to matter.
The burden of proof lies on the person who asserts a fact and who would fail if no evidence at all were given on either side.
So a hole in the evidence hurts whoever needed that fact proved. In a criminal trial that is usually the prosecution.
The court may presume that evidence which could be and is not produced would, if produced, be unfavourable to the person who withholds it.
That is a permission and not a command. The word is may. It bites where evidence was withheld, not merely where some witness was never called.

body.q: The prosecution does not call its one eyewitness and offers no explanation for that. What may the defence ask the court to do?
options: Acquit automatically, because a witness is missing
Order the police to go and produce her at once
Presume that the missing evidence would have been unfavourable to the prosecution
body.why: Illustration (g) to s 114 lets a court presume that withheld evidence would have been unfavourable. It is discretionary, and the unexplained gap is what makes the argument worth running. Nothing about it is automatic.
