lessons.title: Pleading guilty, and bargaining before you do
lessons.summary: A guilty plea can end a case in one morning, and it is the hardest decision in a criminal matter to undo. The Code provides a formal route for bargaining before that plea, and the court still has to be satisfied the plea is a real one.

sections.keypoint: Bargaining before a plea is provided for by the Code; it is not a favour arranged in a corridor.

body.text: Encik Ravi is charged in the Magistrates' Court in Alor Setar. He has been on remand for a week and wants to go home.
Before the case is called, the deputy public prosecutor suggests something. A lesser charge, if Ravi pleads guilty this morning.
That is plea bargaining, and it is not improper. The Criminal Procedure Code provides for it, with an application and a role for the court.

The Criminal Procedure Code provides a procedure for plea bargaining on an application by an accused person, under which the court satisfies itself that the application was made voluntarily before anything is agreed.
body.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593), the plea bargaining provisions inserted by amendment

body.text: Two things can be bargained over. The charge itself, and the sentence the prosecution will ask for.
A conversation in a corridor is not the statutory process. If a bargain is being struck, it belongs on the record, in the form the Code lays down.

sections.keypoint: The court checks four things before it acts on a plea, and any one of them failing means there is no plea.
sections.h: What the court must be satisfied of

body.text: A guilty plea is not simply written down and acted on. The court has work to do before it convicts anybody on one.

items: That the accused understands the charge, put to him in a language he understands.
That he understands what pleading guilty is going to mean for him.
That he admits the facts the prosecution reads out, all of them.
That the plea is his own, and not the product of a promise or a threat.

body.text: The facts are read out for a reason. A plea is worth nothing if the facts read out do not actually amount to the offence charged.
Ravi is charged with theft. The facts read out show he took a bag he honestly believed was his own. The court should not convict him on that plea.

body.prompt: Ravi tells the court he is pleading guilty only because he cannot face another week in the lock-up. What should the court do?
options: Record the conviction, because he did say the word guilty
Adjourn the case for a month and see whether he changes his mind
Decline to act on that plea, because it is not a free and unqualified one
body.reveal: A plea has to be the accused's own, and it has to be unqualified. Saying it to escape remand is a warning the court is meant to hear. The right course is a plea of not guilty, and the case then takes its ordinary path.

sections.keypoint: If mitigation denies part of the offence, the guilty plea has been withdrawn in everything but name.
sections.h: A plea that is not really a plea

body.text: The commonest problem comes after the plea, during mitigation.
Ravi pleads guilty to voluntarily causing hurt. In mitigation his lawyer says he never touched the man at all. That is a denial of the offence.
A plea qualified by what is said afterwards is not an unqualified plea. The court should set it aside and enter a plea of not guilty.
Prepare mitigation before the plea, not after it. Mitigation explains why a person who did it did it. It is not the place to start saying he did not.
There is a real cost in claiming trial, because credit for an early plea is then gone. There is a worse cost in a conviction the court should never have recorded.

sections.keypoint: The sentencing discount is real but never guaranteed, and the plea narrows an appeal to very little.
sections.h: What a guilty plea costs you

body.text: An early plea usually attracts a lighter sentence than a conviction after a full trial. That is the honest reason most pleas are entered.
Usually is not always. No discount is guaranteed, and nobody can promise you a figure. A lawyer who promises one is telling you something he cannot know.
The second cost lands on appeal. A person who pleaded guilty is restricted in what an appeal may attack, and the Code sets that restriction out.
So the plea is close to final. That is what makes it the one decision worth taking slowly, from a cell, in a bad week.

body.q: Ravi wants to plead guilty this morning so that he can sleep at home tonight. What is the one thing he must be told first?
options: That his sentence will certainly be lighter for pleading
That the conviction is close to final, and an appeal after a guilty plea is narrow
That he can change his mind again at any point later on
body.why: The discount is likely but never certain, and it cannot be promised to him. Nor can a plea be undone at will once the court has convicted on it. Finality is the fact he does not yet have, and it is the one that decides this.
